summary:
Azelux is a web application for rapidly comparing two lunar south-pole landing plans—different sites, dates or both. It helps mission planners, educators and the public understand how terrain and schedule changes affect sunlight and direct-to-Earth visibility.

Azelux computes Sun and Earth positions using NASA/JPL SPICE and derives terrain skylines from NASA LOLA elevation data where coverage is available. Side-by-side results combine visibility windows, duration metrics, horizon panoramas, aligned timelines, a best-date finder and interactive 3D terrain. A gap-first view highlights the longest interval without simultaneous Sun and Earth visibility, explains the computed conditions, and lets users download a comparison for offline replay.
Simple and Expert modes support different levels of technical detail. Source provenance, coverage modes, validation evidence and limitations are visible in the application. By making site and date trade-offs easier to explore, Azelux supports rapid assessment when mission schedules change—while clearly distinguishing visibility estimates from power predictions, guaranteed communications or landing-safety certification.
details:
What does your project do?

Azelux helps users compare two lunar landing plans and understand what changes when they choose a different site, landing date or mission duration.

Users can select a location from our sourced site library or enter custom coordinates. The results show sunlight, Earth visibility and the periods when both are visible together. Side-by-side metrics, horizon panoramas, an aligned timeline and a shared scrubber make the differences easier to inspect. A Best Date finder searches a date range and lets users load a candidate directly into Plan B. Maps and an interactive 3D terrain analyser provide additional views of the site.

How does it work?

Azelux uses NASA/JPL SPICE to calculate Sun and Earth positions. Where coverage is available, it uses NASA LOLA elevation data to build a skyline representing the surrounding terrain. It compares each body’s elevation with that skyline to calculate visibility windows, gaps and durations.

Each result identifies its data sources and whether it uses detailed terrain, coarser terrain or a geometric horizon. Metrics include sunlight hours, Earth visibility, simultaneous visibility, the longest dark period and the longest Earth-visibility gap. Green, amber and red verdicts show how each plan meets the user’s selected thresholds.

What benefits does it have, and what impact do you intend?

A landing delay can change a mission’s lighting and Earth-visibility conditions. Azelux brings those changes into one comparison rather than asking users to interpret separate reports.

For mission-planning teams, it supports early exploration of alternatives. For educators and the public, it provides a way to understand why lunar terrain and timing matter. Simple mode emphasizes the main results, while Expert mode exposes detailed metrics, methods and raw data. A glossary, visual tour and guided controller simulator help first-time users get started.

How is the project creative?

One feature we added is a gap-first view. Azelux highlights the longest interval when the Sun and Earth are not both visible, giving users a concrete place to begin.

Explain this interval breaks that gap into periods when the Sun, Earth or both are below the computed horizon. Users can select an event and jump to its position on the timeline. These explanations are derived directly from the calculated windows, without an AI model.

A downloadable offline briefing preserves the comparison, sources and limitations. Users can replay it with a keyboard without an internet connection, or read its static summary with JavaScript disabled. It replays a saved calculation rather than computing new scenarios offline.

What tools, languages and software did you use?

The frontend uses React, TypeScript and Vite, with Three.js and React Three Fiber for 3D views and Leaflet for maps. The Python backend uses FastAPI, SpiceyPy, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio and PyProj for ephemeris and terrain processing.

We used GitHub for collaboration, GitHub Actions for integration checks, pytest for backend tests and Vitest for frontend tests. The application is deployed with its frontend on Vercel and its backend on Render.

What factors did your team consider?

We focused on traceability, usability and clear limits. Sources, terrain coverage, sampling details and validation evidence are visible in the app. We cross-checked ephemeris results against JPL Horizons. A supplementary PGDA comparison passed its stated tolerance using an any-visible-disc rule; the original body-centre comparison remains recorded as a failure. Runtime calculations still use body centres, and that distinction is disclosed.

We also checked keyboard navigation, contrast, reduced motion, responsive layouts and text alternatives. Physical-device, spoken screen-reader and independent usability checks remain part of final acceptance.

Azelux supports planning and education. Its visibility estimates do not predict electrical output, guarantee communications or certify landing safety.
